notes.meaning: The father urges his son to hold tightly to godly instruction and store up God's commands like a valued treasure. To treasure them means to hide them deep within the mind, keeping them safe from harm and loss. When we value God's word above everything else, it protects our daily thoughts.

Obedience brings true life, so the son must protect God's teaching like the pupil of his own eye. The pupil is very tender, essential for sight, and naturally shielded against any injury. In the same way, we should be extremely careful never to damage or neglect God's truth.

God's commands should be tied to the fingers like a reminder ring and engraved on the tablet of the heart. Having them on the fingers keeps daily duty constantly in sight. Writing them on the heart means letting God's truth become part of our deepest loves and desires.

The teacher tells the son to treat God's wisdom like a beloved sister and understanding like a close family member. These terms describe a pure, loving, and familiar bond with godly truth. Loving wisdom this deeply keeps a person's heart satisfied so they do not seek sinful romance.

A close relationship with wisdom serves as a shield against the seductions of an immoral woman. The stranger refers to a woman outside God's covenant boundary of marriage who uses smooth, flattering talk to trap unwary men. God's truth reveals the deceit behind tempting words so a person can escape the trap.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern scholars suggest the stranger or adulteress may represent foreign women, women outside the returned Jewish exile community, or foreign cults rather than only an unfaithful wife.

notes.meaning: Solomon introduces a real-life scene he witnessed from his window through the wooden lattice. The lattice allowed him to watch the street privately while letting in cool air. From this vantage point, he observed human behavior to warn others about hidden moral dangers.

Looking into the street, the writer spots an immature young man who completely lacks good judgment. The word simple does not mean evil, but inexperienced, careless, and easily led astray. Because this youth lacks the inner guard of wisdom, he is open to spiritual disaster.

The young man walks aimlessly near the corner where an immoral woman lives and heads toward her house. Instead of staying far away from danger, he idly wanders right into the neighborhood of temptation. When people have nothing good to do, they often walk straight into trouble.

The young man chooses to walk during twilight, waiting for total darkness to hide what he is doing. People who plan to do wrong often seek the night, hoping that no one will see them. Yet trying to hide in the dark only deceives oneself, because God sees everything.

A woman comes out to meet the young man, dressed in the flashy style of a prostitute and hiding her real motives. Although she is actually a married woman, she dresses boldly and uses deceit to lure him in. Her guarded, cunning heart shows that she does not care about him at all, but only about her own selfish desires.

The woman is described as noisy, stubborn, and restless, refusing to stay inside her own home. She rebels against modesty and self-control, wandering about like an untamed animal. Her unwillingness to care for her home shows her rebellious heart.

She prowls the public spaces, moving from streets to open squares and lurking at every corner. She watches for anyone foolish enough to walk into her trap. Those who reject God's design often wander everywhere looking for trouble.

With shameless boldness, she grabs the young man, kisses him, and speaks directly to him. She does not wait for him to talk or show interest, but takes control of the situation. Her brazen manner reveals an utter lack of shame before God and people.

She invites him by claiming she has just offered peace offerings and paid her vows. Under Old Testament law, the person who gave a peace offering kept part of the meat to share in a celebratory feast that very day. She uses religious duties as an excuse to throw a lavish party and hide her wicked plot.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars suggest the mention of vows and sacrifices may point to pagan rituals or sacred prostitution connected with ancient fertility religions.

notes.meaning: She flatters the young man by claiming she came out specifically to look for him and was thrilled to find him. She acts as though he were the only one she wanted, feeding his pride. Sinners often use intense flattery to make their victims feel uniquely valued.

She describes her couch as richly decorated with beautiful, embroidered linens imported from Egypt. These expensive coverings were meant to dazzle his eyes and promise great physical comfort. She makes sin look luxurious and appealing to weaken his resistance.

She adds that she has perfumed her bed with sweet-smelling spices like myrrh, aloes, and cinnamon. These costly fragrances were intended to stir the senses and create an intoxicating mood. Every detail of her offer is designed to overwhelm his self-control.

She boldly urges him to come and indulge with her in sensual pleasure until morning. She calls this sinful act love, hiding the fact that it is actually selfish lust. Giving in to temptation often means trading lasting honor for a single night of pleasure.

To remove any fear of getting caught, she reassures him that her husband is far away on a long trip. She avoids calling him her husband, coldly referring to him only as the man of the house. She takes advantage of his absence to break her sacred marriage vows.

She explains that her husband took a large bag of money for business and will not return until the full moon. This business journey would keep him away for weeks, so there was no danger of a sudden surprise. Temptation always whispers that no one is watching and that nobody will ever find out.

With endless smooth talk and persuasive flattery, she finally breaks down his defenses and leads him astray. The young man may have felt uneasy at first, but her constant pressure silenced his conscience. When a person listens to sin's flattering lies, moral strength quickly disappears.

He gives in and follows her immediately, like an ox walking calmly into a slaughterhouse. He moves like a foolish criminal being led to the stocks for punishment, completely unaware of the trap. Sin blinds a person so thoroughly that they march cheerfully toward their own ruin.

He hurries into danger like a bird flying straight into a net, unaware that it will cost him his life. The fatal result strikes suddenly, like an arrow shooting through the liver and delivering a deathblow. A moment of forbidden pleasure ends in permanent spiritual and physical destruction.

The teacher pauses to urge all his listeners to pay close attention to his instruction. He addresses them as sons, showing a father's deep concern for their future and safety. Hearing God's warnings is useless unless we carefully take them to heart.

The father commands the young man not to let even his inner thoughts turn toward the adulteress or wander near her paths. Sin begins in the secret desires of the heart before it ever turns into an action. Guarding the mind against wrong thoughts is the best way to keep your feet out of danger.

The warning is reinforced by the sheer number of victims this sin has destroyed. Even mighty heroes and wise leaders, such as Samson and David, suffered terrible wounds because of sexual temptation. If the strongest people have fallen, no one can afford to think they are safe on their own.

Her house is nothing less than an entrance to the grave and the deep chambers of death. Sheol here points to death, the grave, and the final ruin of the soul. Following immorality leads to a dark road from which few ever return.
